articles.title: Musicians are getting really tired of this AI clone ‘bullshit’
articles.summary: Musicians, producers, and others in the industry are reacting to the relentless spread of AI tracks impersonating them.
articles.body: “Not ideal.” “Completely unacceptable.” “Shameless.” “Predatory.” “Some bullshit.” “Total bullshit.” This is how musicians, producers, and others in the industry are describing the relentless spread of AI clones. Of course, AI fakes aren’t new, but as the scammers have gotten more brazen, artists are responding with increasing furor. We got a taste back in 2023 with multiple AI Drake tracks. But, in the last two years, the problem has gotten worse. Everyone from Beyoncé, to experimental composer William Basinski have had fake songs, likely generated by AI, appear to be streaming next to their names. And this week King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard found itself the latest target. Frontman Stu Mackenzie responded with anger, but also resignation, telling The Music, “we are truly doomed.” Spotify has taken steps to address the issue, formalizing its policy against impersonation and removing 75 million spam tracks from its service. But the scale of the problem and the way the current system functions have made it difficult to rein in. Deezer says that 50,000 AI-generated tracks are uploaded to its library per day, accounting for more than 34 percent of the music it ingests. Bad actors take advantage of the fact that music isn’t uploaded directly to Spotify and several other streamers; instead, it goes through a third-party distribution service like DistroKid. It’s unclear what, if any, screening is in place to ensure that someone uploading a song is who they claim to be. (DistroKid did not respond to a request for comment.) This is how the seemingly AI-generated reggaeton song wound up on the Spotify page of William Basinski, an artist who specializes in ambient pieces built around the sounds of colliding black holes, crumbling tape loops, and shortwave radio broadcasts. “It’s total bullshit,” he told The Verge. “Luckily, my label and distributors keep an eye on these idiocies… What a mess.” The response from Luke Temple of Here We Go Magic, whose dormant band was reactivated by AI impostors, was similar. Here We Go Magic haven’t released new music since 2015, but after an AI track made its way onto the band’s Spotify page, Temple told NPR that, “it is so awful.” Similarly, when an AI-generated song called “Name This Night” appeared on the Spotify page for the band Toto in July, guitarist Steve Lukather called it “shameless” in a statement to Ultimate Classic Rock. Now, it’s possible some of these fakes aren’t AI, but AI makes it a hell of a lot quicker and easier to crank them out. While Suno is designed to ignore artist-specific prompts, it’s still easy to generate entire songs with just a few words. "“It’s total bullshit… What a mess.”" - Willam Basinski Breaking Rust is not a clone of a specific artist, but Blanco Brown has accused the creator of modeling it on his vocals. Brown told the AP about someone texting him to let him know that “somebody done typed your name in the AI and made a white version of you. They just used the Blanco, not the Brown.” Brown’s manager, Ryan McMahan, took to LinkedIn, saying, “AI can run a formula. It cannot recreate Blanco’s life experience that he pulls from. It cannot recreate the humanity, the conviction, or the lifetime of emotions that shaped his artistic voice.” Breaking Rust generated attention by climbing to the top of the Billboard Country Digital Song Sales chart, resulting in misleading headlines about AI topping the country charts. But this is not the Country Streaming Songs or Hot Country Songs charts. The Song Sales chart measures things like iTunes purchases, and since hardly anyone actually buys songs on iTunes anymore, “Walk My Walk” was able to hit the top with only 3,000 purchases. It’s possible that whoever is behind the song simply bought their way to the top. Solomon Ray, an AI gospel creation, enjoyed similar chart success and spurred backlash. Christianity Today said Ray “has no soul,” a sentiment echoed by Christian artist Forrest Frank, who said on Instagram that, “AI does not have the Holy Spirit inside of it… It’s really weird to be opening up your spirit to something that has no spirit.” While Solomon Ray does not appear to be a direct clone, there is a real person, Solomon Ray, who is also a singer and a worship leader. Ray (the real one) told Christianity Today, “How much of your heart are you pouring into this? If you’re having AI generate it for you, the answer is zero.” In addition to composing with AI, some are trying to capitalize on the growing furor. A producer named Haven went viral after not-so-subtly suggesting that a song with AI-manipulated vocals was an unreleased Jorja Smith track. Of course, the vocals were not actually Smith’s; they were processed using Suno, and the track was removed from streaming services. Harrison Walker (the man behind Haven) tried to cash in, rerecording the song and even trying to enlist Smith for a remix. Now, Smith and her label FAMM are demanding royalties from Haven. In a statement on Instagram, FAMM said that “creators are collateral damage in the race by governments and corporations towards AI dominance.” The United Musicians and Allied Workers (UMAW) has made no secret about where it stands, calling AI music “exploitation.” Organizer Joey La Neve DeFrancesco told The Verge that “AI has given Spotify and the major labels the ability to fully cut out human artists and the royalties due to them. The streaming giant and the major labels have already cut deals with AI music companies.” [Media: While some of the biggest labels like Warner are warming up to generative AI companies, musicians have found an ally in iHeartRadio. Company president Tom Poleman said on Instagram that “music is a uniquely human art form; creativity, storytelling, and soul that no algorithm can truly replicate.” He pledged that the company would “never play AI-generated music with synthetic vocalists pretending to be human,” and “never use AI-generated on-air personalities or podcasters.” “Sometimes you have to pick a side, and we’re on the side of humans,” he concluded. Holly Herndon is more comfortable with AI than most musicians, having used it extensively, including on her album Proto. But even she has warned artists to be wary of exploitation. On an episode of The Most Interesting Thing in A.I., she said she brought many of her concerns around training data and artists’ rights to some AI companies and “was blown away that they just weren’t really thinking through this issue, they didn’t think people would be upset about it.” DeFrancesco says that, “It’s clear that we need regulation to force streaming services to identify AI content and to remove it from streaming royalty pools.” The United Musicians and Allied Workers is pushing for Congress to pass The Living Wage for Musicians Act, which it says would “protect artists from corporate AI exploitation,” by creating a new royalty paid directly to musicians, by streaming platforms that “would only be paid out to human artists.” For now, the onus is on the artists and their fans to be vigilant. Because, just like videos and photos, music needs to be approached with skepticism in the age of AI.

articles.title: Of course viewers are giving up on Netflix shows
articles.summary: If the streamer wants to keep TikTok from eating its lunch, it has to start giving its shows a chance to build dedicated followings.
articles.body: Even though Netflix is the world’s most popular paid streaming service, the company has been struggling to keep viewers watching its series after their first seasons. Beef — the streamer’s anthology about people locked in feuds — lost 70 percent of its viewership when it returned earlier this year. There seems to be some confusion as to why people aren’t champing at the bit to dive back into once-popular projects like the live-action adaptations of Avatar: The Last Airbender and One Piece. Netflix is reportedly hard at work trying to figure out what, exactly, is prompting subscribers to jump ship in droves. But if you’ve spent any time paying attention to the broader media landscape, the answers — there are a few — are fairly obvious. Some of Netflix’s problems are rooted in its internal practices, like the way it tends to cancel shows right as they start becoming more expensive to produce. It also doesn’t help that, on the whole, the wait between seasons of series has been gradually getting longer, which makes it easier for people to lose interest. But Netflix also has to deal with the reality that competitors like TikTok and YouTube are capturing people’s attention in ways that it simply can’t. It only took a few years for adults in the US to begin spending just about the same amount of time scrolling through TikTok as they do watching things on Netflix. This is undoubtedly part of the reason why the streamer has been so aggressive about getting into games, live sports, and video podcasts. Netflix also has plans to experiment with short-form content that sounds like it’s meant to be consumed in the moments when people have time to kill. But the simple fact that TikTok and YouTube are free makes them significantly more accessible than Netflix, and it seems very unlikely that short videos will be enough to get people signing up for the paid service. In addition to viewers spending more time on other platforms, Netflix also has to contend with the way the streaming wars have fundamentally altered people’s relationships with episodic television. When the platform first launched, appointment watching was still a thing and people made an effort to keep up with programs from week to week. But Netflix’s binge model trained audiences to cluster around shows for brief windows before moving on to the Next Big Thing that folks are yapping about on social media. The binge model made it difficult for Netflix’s shows to maintain long-term engagement or generate the word-of-mouth buzz that turns people on the fence into paying customers. And while the company has had some success releasing projects on a weekly basis, it’s a bit too late in the game for that strategy to solve its fall-off problem. Something else that Netflix has to take into consideration is that, sometimes, people just stop watching shows when they aren’t particularly enjoyable. As much as we all loved Stranger Things in its early days, the show became an unwieldy mess by its final season. Stranger Things was a big enough phenomenon that its diminishing quality didn’t exactly hurt its overall viewership. But the same can’t be said for some of Netflix’s newer would-be flagship shows like Avatar, which came out of the gate limping and quickly drew ire from fans of the original animated series. What Netflix needs to really turn this ship around is to focus on producing the kind of programming that gets people locked in, and then actually sticking with it once shows manage to build dedicated audiences. This will take time, patience, and money on the company’s part, which isn’t exactly the kind of strategy that gets stockholders salivating. But it’s really the only way that Netflix can hope to climb its way out of this hole and keep other platforms from eating its lunch.

articles.title: 'Scene' box office collection day 10: Suriya and Naslen's film earns over three times 'Aavesham'; worldwide gross crosses Rs 242 cr
articles.summary: Suriya and Naslen's 'Scene' continues its impressive theatrical run, maintaining a strong hold during its second week.
articles.body: Suriya and Naslen's 'Scene' continues its impressive theatrical run, maintaining a strong hold during its second week. The film has crossed another major milestone, taking its worldwide gross collection to Rs 242.05 cr within ten days. Its latest earnings have also placed it considerably ahead of director Jithu Madhavan's previous film, 'Aavesham', at the corresponding stage of their theatrical runs.'Scene' records a strong Day 10 collection despite a slight declineAccording to Sacnilk, 'Scene' collected Rs 9.30 cr in India net on its tenth day, registering a marginal 2.1% decline from the previous day's Rs 9.50 cr. The Tamil version contributed Rs 7.10 cr through 3,123 shows, while the Telugu version added Rs 2.20 cr from 1,253 shows. Together, the film registered 4,376 shows across both language versions.The latest figures have taken its cumulative India net collection to Rs 136.50 cr. Its domestic gross total stands at Rs 158.55 cr. The film collected Rs 111.70 cr net during its opening week. Its second-week earnings have now reached Rs 24.80 cr, covering the first three days of the week. The overall show count across its ten-day theatrical run has reached 52,077.Overseas collections push worldwide total beyond Rs 240 crThe film's overseas performance has played a significant role in its overall box office growth. International markets contributed Rs 4 cr on Day 10, taking the cumulative overseas gross to Rs 83.50 cr. With its domestic and international earnings combined, the worldwide collection has reached Rs 242.05 cr.The overseas market accounts for approximately 34.5% of the film's combined India and international gross. Domestic markets contribute the remaining 65.5%.The Tamil version continued to account for the majority of the film's domestic earnings. Its cumulative India net collection stands at Rs 109.95 cr, representing 80.5% of the total. The Telugu version has contributed Rs 26.55 cr, accounting for the remaining 19.5%.The Tamil version recorded an overall theatre occupancy of 50.06% on Day 10. Morning shows registered 34.92%, while afternoon screenings improved to 59.08%. Evening shows recorded the highest occupancy at 61.69%, followed by 44.54% during night screenings.Tamil Nadu contributes the highest state-wise gross collectionTamil Nadu remained the biggest contributor to the film's state-wise gross earnings, collecting Rs 5 cr on Day 10. Andhra Pradesh and Telangana together added Rs 2.50 cr, while Kerala contributed Rs 1.85 cr. Karnataka recorded Rs 1.25 cr, and the remaining Indian territories accounted for Rs 20 lakh. The combined state-wise gross collection for the day was Rs 10.80 cr.'Scene' earns over three times 'Aavesham' at the same stageThe comparison with Jithu Madhavan's earlier film 'Aavesham' highlights the difference in their box office performances. On its tenth day, 'Aavesham' collected Rs 4.55 cr in India net through 1,657 shows. Its cumulative domestic net collection stood at Rs 38.70 cr, while the India gross reached Rs 44.51 cr.The film also earned Rs 1.70 cr from overseas markets on the corresponding day. This took its international gross to Rs 35.50 cr and worldwide collection to Rs 80.01 cr. An estimated 355,147 tickets were sold on Day 10, taking its total ticket sales throughout the theatrical run to 3,112,913.In comparison, 'Scene' has accumulated more than three times the worldwide gross collected by 'Aavesham' at this stage. With its second week underway, the Suriya and Naslen starrer continues to add to its impressive theatrical total. The film also has Nasriya Nazim in the female lead.DISCLAIMER: The box office numbers and the data in this article are compiled from public and industry sources. articles.title: Amitabh Bachchan recalls near-fatal incident where he almost drowned while kayaking in Nepal: 'Nobody came to my rescue, imagine...'
articles.summary: Amitabh Bachchan has often shared interesting anecdotes from his life on 'Kaun Banega Crorepati', giving viewers a glimpse into experiences beyond his
articles.body: Amitabh Bachchan has often shared interesting anecdotes from his life on 'Kaun Banega Crorepati', giving viewers a glimpse into experiences beyond his film career. In an upcoming episode of the quiz show, the veteran actor recounts a frightening incident from a film shoot in Nepal, where a kayaking adventure nearly turned fatal after his boat capsized.During his conversation with a contestant, Bachchan revealed that he was in Nepal for a shooting schedule when someone suggested he try kayaking, describing it as a wonderful experience. However, the actor soon discovered that the water sport was far more challenging and dangerous than he had imagined. He explained that the kayak was extremely narrow and that getting into it alone took him nearly 45 minutes.Although he was hesitant initially, Bachchan eventually decided to give the activity a shot. Getting into the kayak itself proved to be quite a task. Things took a much more alarming turn when he made an incorrect move while paddling, causing the boat to overturn.Recalling the incident, he said, "You have to paddle in the correct direction, and what happened was that I was supposed to turn the boat one way, but I turned it the other way, and the boat capsized. When it overturned, I had been told that if such a situation arose, I should push my hands upwards from underwater so that the boat would right itself. And if that didn’t work, I should wave both my hands vigorously underwater so that the people around would realise that someone was drowning. So I was waving my hands vigorously underwater, trying to make my way out. After all, one cannot hold one’s breath for that long."The actor further revealed that despite his desperate attempts to signal for help, nobody came to his rescue immediately. Adding to the irony of the situation, the film's lead actor was himself struggling to stay afloat while the shoot was underway.He recalled, "You won’t believe it, but nobody came to rescue me. On top of that, we were shooting a film, and the film's hero himself was drowning. Imagine they would have had to continue working with the other hero. However, someone standing near the waterfall realised that something was seriously wrong, and somehow managed to pull me out. It was quite an ordeal, I tell you. It takes three to four people just to pull someone out of there, and even getting me out proved to be quite difficult."Despite the frightening experience, Bachchan narrated the incident with his characteristic humour, remembering how difficult it was for the people around to pull him out of the water.'Kaun Banega Crorepati' remains one of India's most popular television quiz shows, with Bachchan at the helm for several seasons. articles.title: Tiger Shroff firing case: MCOCA court sends five accused to judicial custody and Suneha Pandit to Crime Branch custody over money trail till November 21
articles.summary: The Mumbai Crime Branch on Monday produced six accused in the Tiger Shroff firing case before the MCOCA court.
articles.body: The Mumbai Crime Branch on Monday produced six accused in the Tiger Shroff firing case before the MCOCA court. Five were sent to judicial custody, while Suneha Pandit was remanded to police custody until November 21.Court orders custody for six accusedAccording to the IANS report, the six were presented after their police custody ended on November 16. They are among 13 people arrested so far in the case. Suneha is the wife of absconding accused Abhishek, who reportedly managed the bank accounts of the entire network while living abroad.Money trail under the scannerInvestigators say money for the firing was routed through these accounts, and they have also found details of funds reaching Suneha. Police have noted that over 20 QR codes were used in the conspiracy. They say it is necessary to question those linked to these codes to learn about their role in the transactions. Probe findings also suggest that money was sent to certain vendors whose QR codes were used.Police sought Suneha’s custody to trace the financial links, identify other people involved and establish the connections between the accused.What happened to Tiger ShroffThe ‘Baaghi’ actor recently had a narrow escape when three men on motorcycles fired at his car in Mumbai’s Juhu area on October 19. Tiger was reported to be safe, but his driver was injured.Tiger Shroff's work frontTiger Shroff was last seen in ‘Baaghi 4’, directed by A Harsha, which released in September 2025 and also starred Sanjay Dutt. It did not do well at the box office. He next stars in ‘Lag Ja Gale’ with Janhvi Kapoor and Lakshya, a Dharma Productions film releasing on May 14, 2027. The actor has also confirmed that ‘Rambo’ is back on track after years of delay. He has reportedly signed Ram Madhvani’s spiritual action thriller, with a large part to be shot in Japan. articles.title: Sir Tom Jones to headline Blenheim Palace Festival
articles.summary: Sir Tom Jones set to headline Blenheim Palace Festival 2027, with Nile Rodgers & CHIC as guests.
articles.body:
Sir Tom Jones has been announced as the 5th headliner of Oxfordshire's Blenheim Palace Festival 2027, with Nile Rodgers & CHIC joining him as special guests.

The Palace in Woodstock will host 5 nights of music in June and July next year, with performances from headliners Mariah Carey , Shania Twain , Alex Warren and David Gray.

Heather Carter, managing director of visitor attraction at Blenheim Palace, said it will be an "unforgettable night for fans", as "they're both true musical icons", looking ahead to a "very special evening of music."

The UNESCO World Heritage site was home to the festival for the first time this year, which saw performanes from Katy Perry, Michael Bublé and Teddy Swims.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

Sir Tom, 86, said that he feared his life was "over", after he was admitted to hospital, and had to cancel or reschedule some dates on his US 'Come Gather Round' leg of the tour, after coming down with a "bad case of the flu", he says.

In his last series as a coach on 'The Voice', which is the latest series, he mentored Welsh Singer Cate McHugh to be crowned winner.

But Sir Tom previously revealed on social media that ITV had "fired" him as a judge on the show,. That saw fellow 'The Voice UK' judge, Will.i.am's, support a petition for Sir Tom to be reinstated.

His 60-year career has seen hits such as It's Not Unusual, What's New Pussycat?, Delilah and Green, Green Grass of Home and he has also announced homecoming gigs in Wales next year as part of a Come Gather Round world tour.

articles.title: ‘24’ star Kiefer Sutherland claims self-defense in Uber driver assault lawsuit, calls suit ‘frivolous’
articles.summary: Kiefer Sutherland claims self-defense in his response to an Uber driver's assault lawsuit, calling the allegations frivolous and filed to harass him.
articles.body: Kiefer Sutherland is pushing back against an Uber driver’s assault allegations, arguing that any actions he took were in self-defense and accusing the driver of pursuing the lawsuit to harass him. In court documents filed on Nov. 10 and obtained by Fox News Digital, the "24" actor denied wrongdoing in the case brought by Rafael Manvelyan in Los Angeles Superior Court. His attorneys argued that Sutherland reasonably believed he faced an imminent threat and asked that the amended complaint be dismissed with prejudice. The response comes months after Sutherland’s Jan. 12 arrest following an alleged altercation with a rideshare driver near Sunset Boulevard and Fairfax Avenue in Los Angeles. According to arrest records obtained by Fox News Digital, the 59-year-old actor was released later that day on $50,000 bond. KIEFER SUTHERLAND ALLEGEDLY PUNCHED, CHOKED UBER DRIVER BEFORE CHASE THROUGH LA STREETS: REPORT Manvelyan alleged in his amended complaint that Sutherland appeared intoxicated, threatened him and attacked him during the ride, including placing him in a chokehold and striking him repeatedly. He claimed physical injuries, emotional distress, lost earnings and medical expenses. In dispatch audio previously obtained by Fox News Digital, police could be heard discussing an alleged chase involving the suspect, believed to be Sutherland, and the person reporting the incident. The initial call came in around 12:15am, and a subsequent update indicated the suspect had stopped chasing the person. No further," a voice on the recording said. The Los Angeles Police Department told Fox News Digital at the time that officers responded to a report of an assault involving a rideshare driver. "The investigation determined that the suspect, later identified as Kiefer Sutherland, entered a rideshare vehicle, physically assaulted the driver (the victim), and made criminal threats toward the victim," police said. WATCH: KIEFER SUTHERLAND FACING CRIMINAL CHARGES OVER ALLEGED ATTACK ON RIDE-SHARE DRIVER In his response to the amended complaint, Sutherland’s attorneys broadly denied "each and every allegation" and asserted self-defense. "Defendant acted reasonably and used only such force as was reasonably necessary under the circumstances." The filing does not describe specific actions by Manvelyan that allegedly prompted that belief. Sutherland’s legal team also challenged the driver’s reasons for bringing the case, calling the claims "frivolous and groundless." "Furthermore, this suit is being pursued in bad faith for vexatious reasons for the purpose of harassing Defendant," the filing states. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? "Plaintiff’s claims for emotional distress injuries and damages are barred, in whole or in part, to the extent that such damages are attributable to preexisting or concurrent psychological conditions, unrelated stressors or other independent causes, rather than any act or omission of Defendant," they wrote. The filing does not provide medical records or identify a psychological diagnosis. articles.title: Jennifer Love Hewitt Reveals the Secret to 13 Years of Marriage with Husband Brian Hallisay (Exclusive)
articles.summary: “It’s a long time with another person, it really is,” the actress tells PEOPLE of marking her 13th wedding anniversary on Nov. 20
articles.body:
Jennifer Love Hewitt exclusively tells PEOPLE how she and husband Brian Hallisay keep their romance alive after 13 years of marriage

"I don't ever expect him to choose me. I want to earn that choice every day," she says

The 9-1-1 actress celebrated the launch of her "Raine with Love" collaboration with jewelry brand Raine Calabasas on Nov. 14

Jennifer Love Hewitt 's "heart still flutters" after 13 years of marriage with husband Brian Hallisay .

While catching up with PEOPLE on Saturday, Nov. 14 at the celebration for her "Raine with Love" collaboration with jewelry brand Raine Calabasas , the 9-1-1 actress, 47, reflected on 13 years of marriage with the 48-year-old investment banker-turned-actor just days ahead of their anniversary. The couple tied the knot in Nov. 20, 2013.

"In Hollywood, it's like 150 [years]," she quips of the time they've spent together. "It's a long time with another person. It really is."

"I think that, you know, it ebbs and flows," she continues of their romantic spark. "I think for us, it's a choice every day. And that's the romantic part. I don't ever expect him to choose me. I want to earn that choice every day."

Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.

Hewitt goes on to admit that, when her husband is gone for any period of time, her heart "still flutters a little bit" when he returns.

"I still want him to be right there. And it's a good feeling," she says. "I think we just feel lucky and we keep it going."

"I didn't have that growing up myself, and so I feel very fortunate that I have it," she adds. "He's a really good partner. He's a great dad. And he's just a good man. And so I feel very lucky to have him."

Hewitt and Hallisay share three kids : Autumn, 12, Atticus, 11, and Aidan, 5.

The couple first crossed paths while filming the unaired pilot of the 2011 television series Love Bites , PEOPLE previously reported. Years later, they reconnected on The Client List while playing estranged spouses.

While celebrating their 12th anniversary last year, Hewitt described Hallisay as the "man of my dreams" while sharing a few sweet selfies to Instagram.

Even in December 2024, the I Know What You Did Last Summer actress expressed to PEOPLE just how " proud " she was of their family after 11 years of marriage.

"We, I think, struggle like most parents with three kids and full-time jobs and all of the things to find our time, but I really do wake up and choose Brian every day, and I would choose him every time," she said at the time. "I genuinely feel that way, even when he makes me crazy. And he continues to choose me, thank God. I am always so profoundly happy that my kids are half him."

articles.title: David Broncano estalla contra Vox tras su denuncia a 'La Revuelta' ante la Junta Electoral Central: "No vamos a concederles ni una más"
articles.standfirst: El presentador se mostró visiblemente enfadado por la polémica reacción a la entrevista realizada a Santiago Abascal
articles.summary: El presentador se mostró visiblemente enfadado por la polémica reacción a la entrevista realizada a Santiago Abascal
articles.body: Este lunes, 16 de noviembre, ‘La Revuelta', programa que presenta y dirige David Broncano en el ‘access prime time’ regresó a emisión una semana más. En esta ocasión, las invitadas al Teatro Albéniz de Madrid fueron Dulceida, Carolina Iglesias y Paula Vázquez, que se encargarán de presentar los Premios Ídolo 2026 en RTVE el próximo miércoles, 2 de diciembre. Sin embargo, antes de darles la bienvenida, sacó a escena la entrevista de hace justo una semana a Santiago Abascal, líder de Vox, en su programa. Cabe recalcar que la formación verde trajo a su público y Broncano accedió a ello, para evitar cualquier tipo de problema relacionado, según comentaron ellos. La charla ha traído cola en los últimos días. El partido que comanda Abascal denuncia que la entrevista fue cortada unos 40 minutos y, por ello, no acudieron a ‘The Wild Project’, el pódcast de Jordi Wild pese a haberse comprometido a ir. En este contexto, Vox denunció a RTVE ante la Junta Electoral por ese ‘corte’ a la entrevista, ya que sostienen que se abordaron cuestiones como la sanidad, la inmigración y los servicios públicos y no se emitió. Por ello, afirman que esto vulnera los principios de neutralidad informativa y pluralismo político y exigen que publiquen la entrevista íntegra y que entreguen una copia de la misma al partido. Una vez puestos en situación, el presentador sacó el tema a escena: “Me arrepiento de tantas cosas el lunes, encima me vaciló y ahora nos denuncian ante la Junta Electoral. Se han aprovechado del programa para mi desgracia y ahora me dicen que hemos secuestrado 40 minutos que no se han emitido, algo que hemos hecho en 1.500 programas que llevamos”. “A Sánchez le cortamos 50 minutos. Si quitamos estos minutos de la entrevista y encima emitimos lo que emitimos y quedamos como la mie***, no creo que cambie nada, no hemos ocultado nada. Lo que está claro es que no vamos a concederles ni una más nunca, nos la han liado y encima han usado esto contra Jordi Wild”, siguió diciendo visiblemente enfadado. Por último, Broncano también quiso aclarar las declaraciones de Abascal sobre una supuesta obligación de RTVE para realizar la entrevista. El líder de Vox aseguró que nadie le había obligado a acudir al programa y que la decisión había sido responsabilidad del propio equipo de 'La Revuelta': “Eso de que me habían obligado a hacer la entrevista es mentira. La responsabilidad es nuestra, podría haber dicho que no viniera, me equivoqué y es cosa nuestra”.

articles.title: In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
articles.summary: Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how manosphere influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
articles.body: Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be. Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making. Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him. [Media: The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings. As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances. As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous. [Image: Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming. Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need. What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content. All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

articles.title: Carmen Machi, entre su pasión por el Real Madrid y su admiración por Rafa Nadal: "Soy exagerada"
articles.standfirst: La actriz ha sido la invitada de Pablo Motos este lunes en 'El Hormiguero'
articles.summary: La actriz ha sido la invitada de Pablo Motos este lunes en 'El Hormiguero'
articles.body: 'El Hormiguero' ha empezado la semana con la visita de la actriz Carmen Machi, quien ha presentado la segunda temporada de 'Celeste', que se estrenará en Movistar Plus+ este jueves, día 19 de noviembre. PABLO MOTOS. Antes de hablar de Celeste, enhorabuena por el Premio Nacional de Cinematografía. ¿Cómo recibiste la noticia? CARMEN MACHI. Muchísimas gracias. La verdad es que me quedé completamente sorprendida. Es un premio que jamás me hubiera imaginado recibir. Además, me llamó el ministro para comunicármelo y, sinceramente, pensé que era una broma. Acababa de coincidir con él una semana antes porque me habían entregado la Medalla al Mérito de las Bellas Artes y creí que me llamaba por alguna cuestión relacionada con aquello. Cuando me dio la noticia, me quedé completamente flipada. Tardé bastante en reaccionar porque es una responsabilidad enorme. Solo el nombre ya impone muchísimo: Premio Nacional de Cinematografía. PABLO MOTOS. Presentas la segunda temporada de 'Celeste', que llega a Movistar Plus+ este jueves. ¿Qué va a encontrarse el espectador? CARMEN MACHI. Esta temporada viajamos al pasado. Es una precuela de acontecimientos que ya se mencionaban en la primera entrega. Mi personaje vuelve a investigar un gran caso fiscal, esta vez relacionado con un futbolista del Real Madrid. Lo curioso es que el público ya sabe cómo termina todo porque en la primera temporada se hacía referencia a esa inspección. La gracia no está en descubrir el final, sino en ver cómo sucede todo. Diego San José lo explica muy bien: eliminamos la tensión de qué ocurrirá para centrarnos en el viaje. Y tengo que decir que la segunda temporada es buenísima. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Fue complicado recuperar al personaje después de tanto tiempo? CARMEN MACHI. Habían pasado dos años desde el rodaje anterior y muchas cosas habían cambiado. Incluso el perro parecía otro. Yo bromeaba diciendo que me habían cambiado al perro, aunque en realidad era el mismo. Lo que pasa es que dos años para un perro son muchos años. Había cambiado de personalidad, ya ni me conocía. Eso sí, seguía siendo muy profesional. PABLO MOTOS. Has dicho alguna vez que te gusta trabajar con peluca. ¿Por qué? CARMEN MACHI. Porque una buena peluca te da muchísimo del personaje. Te la colocas y ya tienes hecho gran parte del trabajo. El aspecto físico influye muchísimo en cómo te colocas, cómo te mueves y cómo te relacionas con el personaje. Pero tiene que ser una peluca muy buena y muy bien puesta. Cuando eso ocurre, ayuda muchísimo a construir la interpretación. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Es verdad que las mejores son de pelo natural? CARMEN MACHI. Sí, de pelo natural. Y eso me recuerda una historia muy bonita que viví durante el rodaje de Amor de madre en Mauricio. Allí habían sufrido un vertido de combustible muy grave que amenazaba los arrecifes de coral. Muchas mujeres decidieron cortarse el pelo para fabricar barreras que ayudaran a contener el fuel. Cuando volví meses después, me llamó mucho la atención ver que todas llevaban el pelo mucho más corto. Gracias a aquella iniciativa consiguieron proteger gran parte de los corales. Es una historia preciosa. PABLO MOTOS. En 'Celeste' interpretas a una inspectora de Hacienda que investiga a un futbolista, y tú eres una gran aficionada al Real Madrid. ¿Hasta qué punto? CARMEN MACHI. Muchísimo. Si me preguntas del cero al diez, soy un diez de madridista. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Tanto como para modificar un rodaje? CARMEN MACHI. Sí. Ha ocurrido más de una vez. He llegado a revisar el plan de trabajo y preguntar: "¿El Madrid juega a las siete? ¿Y yo tengo la última secuencia a las siete?". Lo hablo con producción y buscamos soluciones. Soy muy profesional y voy a trabajar, pero también soy muy madridista. Así que, ante la duda, a veces lo cambian. PABLO MOTOS. También has confesado ser una gran admiradora de Rafa Nadal. CARMEN MACHI. Sí, muchísimo. Lo admiro profundamente. Es una persona que me ha dado momentos de enorme felicidad viendo sus partidos. Me gusta tanto que incluso he evitado conocerlo de verdad. Tengo cierta mitomanía y me pongo muy nerviosa. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Nunca has estado cerca de conocerlo? CARMEN MACHI. Sí, y precisamente por eso tengo una anécdota muy ridícula. Estaba en el Mutua Madrid Open y coincidí con Alejandro Sanz. Me saludó y, de repente, me dijo que cuando terminara el partido iban a recoger a Rafa Nadal para irse a cenar y que me uniera a ellos. Me puse tan nerviosa que inventé una excusa absurda, dije que no tenía hambre y, en cuanto terminó el partido, salí corriendo para que nadie volviera a insistir. Hice el ridículo más grande del mundo. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Qué significa Nadal para ti? CARMEN MACHI. Muchísimo. Lo admiro como deportista y como persona. Es alguien muy importante en mi vida, aunque no le conozca personalmente. Ha provocado muchos momentos de felicidad. He sufrido con sus lesiones, he perdido el sueño viéndole competir y me he llevado alegrías inmensas con sus victorias. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Cómo vives los partidos? CARMEN MACHI. Muy intensamente. Mi mejor plan es llegar a casa y ver fútbol sola. No soporto que me hablen durante el partido. Nada de preguntas ni comentarios. Yo estoy concentrada viendo el encuentro. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Sufres mucho? CARMEN MACHI. Muchísimo. Soy exagerada. Con Rafa Nadal he llegado a tirarme de cabeza por el sofá de los nervios. Me han grabado haciendo cosas rarísimas. He pasado noches sin dormir y días sin comer por la preocupación cuando se lesionaba. PABLO MOTOS. Aunque mucha gente te identifica con Aída, ¿con cuál de las dos series te quedas, con 'Aída' o con 'Siete vidas'? CARMEN MACHI. Con 'Siete vidas'. Y lo digo sin despreciar a 'Aída', porque 'Aída' forma parte de mi familia y de mi vida. Pero en 'Siete vidas' fui inmensamente feliz. Era un grupo maravilloso, nos divertíamos muchísimo y marcó un antes y un después en mi carrera. Además, fue el origen de todo lo que vino después. PABLO MOTOS. Hace un tiempo hablaste públicamente de los ataques de ansiedad que sufriste. ¿Cómo recuerdas aquella etapa? CARMEN MACHI. Fue muy dura. A veces creemos que todo está bien porque seguimos trabajando y haciendo nuestra vida, pero hay cosas que se van acumulando. En mi caso también estaba atravesando un duelo y llegó un momento en que mi cuerpo dijo basta. Empecé a sufrir ataques de ansiedad y ataques de pánico muy fuertes. Estaba rodando una película y acababa prácticamente cada noche en urgencias. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Llegó un momento en que tuviste que parar? CARMEN MACHI. Sí. Estuve entre cuatro y cinco meses sin trabajar. No podía salir de casa. Había días en los que me preparaba para acudir a una promoción convencida de que estaba bien y, justo al abrir la puerta, era incapaz de salir. No podía hablar con nadie ni enfrentarme a situaciones cotidianas. Fue terrible. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Qué te ayudó a superarlo? CARMEN MACHI. Lo primero fue entender qué me estaba pasando. Después, pedir ayuda. Y aquí quiero reivindicar algo muy importante: viva la terapia y viva la medicación cuando está prescrita por profesionales. Los psiquiatras y los psicólogos me ayudaron muchísimo. A veces la química es necesaria y no pasa nada por decirlo. PABLO MOTOS. ¿Qué consejo darías a quienes estén pasando por algo parecido? CARMEN MACHI. Hablarlo. Parece una tontería, pero verbalizarlo tiene un efecto enorme. Cuando dices "me está dando un ataque de ansiedad" o "me está ocurriendo esto", gran parte del miedo desaparece. En mi caso fue fundamental. También ayuda salir del entorno en el que te está ocurriendo, respirar, escuchar lo que te está pasando y no intentar ocultarlo. Reconocerlo es el primer paso para empezar a curarte.

articles.title: 'Bridgerton' star boycotts upcoming 'Harry Potter' TV show over author JK Rowling's transgender views
articles.summary: Actress Nicola Coughlan, a vocal supporter of transgender rights, said she'd never join HBO Max's "Harry Potter" series despite loving the original books.
articles.body: "Bridgerton" actress Nicola Coughlan declared Thursday she would never watch or appear in Warner Bros. Discovery and HBO Max's upcoming "Harry Potter" series because of author J.K. Rowling's views on transgender issues. In an interview with The Observer, Coughlan spoke about her political activism, including fundraising for Palestinian causes, marching for abortion rights and advocating for transgender rights. Coughlan said she would not watch or participate in the upcoming adaptation of Rowling's fantasy series, despite her love for the original books. The show is scheduled to premiere Dec. 25. "I will not be watching the new ‘Harry Potter’ show and I would never be in it," Coughlan said. "Look, I know people that are involved in those shows, and they're nice people and whatever, but it's not for me." HBO’S 'HARRY POTTER' GETS A HARD NO FROM 'BLACK MIRROR,' 'LOKI' DIRECTORS OVER JK ROWLING’S TRANS VIEWS Rowling has defended women-only spaces and opposed some transgender rights policies. She also previously criticized Coughlan. In 2025, Coughlan criticized Rowling for celebrating a unanimous ruling by the U.K. Supreme Court that the terms "woman" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex. The ruling addressed the interpretation of the law, including provisions governing single-sex spaces. Coughlan wrote on Instagram, "Keep your new ‘Harry Potter’ lads. Wouldn’t touch it with a 10-foot pole." JK ROWLING REFUSES TO BACK DOWN IN ESSAY CALLING TRANS ACTIVISM 'ELITIST TO ITS CORE' Following Coughlan's remarks, Rowling wrote on X that she did not know who Coughlan or actor Pedro Pascal was. Both actors had criticized Rowling. In her interview with The Observer, Coughlan responded to Rowling's comments. "Me, I could believe," Coughlan said. "But Pedro Pascal? You know who Pedro Pascal is, girl. Like, please." Fox News Digital reached out to Warner Bros. Discovery and Rowling for comment but did not immediately receive a response. ROYAL FAMILY FACES BACKLASH FROM CRITICS AFTER QUEEN CAMILLA HOSTS J.K. ROWLING Christian Toto, host of the "Hollywood in Toto" podcast, told Fox News Digital that Coughlan's comments likely "won't move the needle a millimeter" on the upcoming series, which he described as one of the most hotly anticipated shows in a while. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "This is the easiest and laziest virtue signal possible for a less than recognizable actress. It's just one of many positions Hollywood is supposed to endorse," Toto told Fox News Digital. "End ICE. Trump is a dictator. J.K. Rowling is wrong on trans issues but they can't explain why. There's nothing brave or unexpected in Coughlan's comments. It's almost like she's reading from a script."

articles.title: Robert Pattinson may be too famous for James Bond. That could be a good thing.
articles.summary: Some fans think Robert Pattinson is already everywhere. Bond experts explain why his franchise fame and range could work in his favor as Bond.
articles.body:
The long-running search for the new James Bond ended Monday with the announcement that Robert Pattinson will take over as the suave spy.

Speculation around casting has swirled since Daniel Craig bade farewell to 007 in 2021's No Time to Die . Jack Lowden, Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Nicholas Hoult were reportedly contenders , while Idris Elba spent years fielding rumors and fans debated whether a woman should step into the role.

Pattinson already has another supersize gig: Batman , which will release a sequel in 2028. And for some viewers, that makes Hollywood's most anticipated casting announcement a letdown.

"Do we really have such a shortage of actors that we need the same handful of guys playing every iconic character?" Jake Ross, who covers movies via Breakdowns & Blockbusters, wrote on X.

Pattinson is, after all, everywhere . The British actor, 40, became a global star through the Twilight franchise after playing Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire . This year, he's appeared in The Drama , The Odyssey and Primetime , with Dune: Part Three still to come. Now he's adding Bond to a résumé that already includes Edward Cullen and Batman — two characters big enough to define an actor's career.

One commenter on Yahoo's casting story questioned the choice while acknowledging Pattinson's talent: "I would have preferred a lesser-known actor to take over the franchise — someone who doesn't come with a lot of preconceptions and who could have benefitted from a (potentially) huge career boost." Still, the reader added, Pattinson "has the acting chops."

"The casting of Pattinson is a tectonic shift for this franchise," Colin Burnett, an associate professor at Washington University in St. Louis who has taught a "James Bond and the Modern Media Franchise" course, tells Yahoo. "Never before has a star at the peak of his career been cast in the role."

That's not to say they've all been unknowns, says James Chapman, author of Licence to Thrill: A Cultural History of the James Bond Films . Previous Bonds brought their own screen identities to the role.

Craig and Sean Connery were actors on the cusp of stardom, while Roger Moore and Pierce Brosnan were established television stars, Chapman says.

George Lazenby, the Australian model who played Bond in On Her Majesty's Secret Service , "was really the only 'unknown' cast as Bond," says Chapman, emeritus professor of film studies at the University of Leicester.

For all their previous success, the actors were stepping into a role bigger than themselves.

"The producers always regarded the character of Bond as a star," he says.

Chapman doesn't see Pattinson's association with other franchises affecting the way audiences view him as Bond. Film historian Steven Jay Rubin, author of The James Bond Movie Encyclopedia , goes further: He sees Pattinson's franchise familiarity as an advantage.

"It elevates the weight of the property to an important audience — the non-Bond fan, who would be less inclined to gravitate towards an unknown," Rubin says . "This applies particularly to the younger generation that isn't steeped in Bond history."

Rubin thinks that Batman gives Pattinson "credibility as a genre hero." With movies, TV shows, games, streaming and live events competing for attention, Rubin argues, an established star can help a project stand out.

"Matching Pattinson to the Bond brand is a smart choice," Rubin says. "I don't think anyone will mark him down because he's Batman."

There is precedent for audiences embracing one actor in several supersize roles: Harrison Ford was already Han Solo when he became Indiana Jones, then went on to play Jack Ryan in two films. Robert Downey Jr. played Sherlock Holmes while starring as Iron Man.

"In this age of franchises, a success in one franchise series can boost the same actors in others," Chapman says.

Burnett says that Pattinson has developed an identity beyond his franchises anyway.

"He's a versatile actor who continually reinvents himself in role after role," Burnett says, pointing to his very different performances in The Drama and The Odyssey this year.

The test will be less about how many familiar characters he plays than what he brings to this one.

Rubin says the actor has "the air of mystery about him, which I believe serves Bond well."

Chapman says audiences can embrace Pattinson as Bond "provided he gets some good scripts and lines" in the Denis Villeneuve-directed project.

He also considers Pattinson "a good enough actor to make his Bond very different from his Batman."

Even if both have a thing for gadgets, cool cars and saving the day.

articles.title: Teatro Municipal de Uberlândia pode mudar de nome novamente; entenda  | G1
articles.standfirst: Prefeitura anuncia licitação para marcas que queira associar o nome ao teatro. O valor mínimo previsto é de de pouco mais de R$ 11 milhões e contrato com duração de 10 anos.
articles.summary: A Prefeitura de Uberlândia abriu licitação de R$ 11 milhões para empresas interessadas no naming rights do Teatro Municipal, obra icônica de Oscar Niemeyer.
articles.body:
Marcas podem enviar propostas para se associarem ao nome do Teatro Municipal de Uberl — Foto: Adreana Oliveira/g1

A Prefeitura de Uberlândia publicou nesta terça-feira (17) o edital para escolher uma empresa que poderá associar sua marca ao Teatro Municipal de Uberlândia Odelmo Leão. A licitação prevê valor mínimo de R$ 11.189.817,70 e contrato com duração de 10 anos.

A concorrência pública será realizada na modalidade eletrônica, pelo critério de maior oferta. A sessão pública está marcada para 22 de fevereiro de 2027, às 9h, pela plataforma Licitanet.

A iniciativa é chamada de naming rights, expressão em inglês usada para definir o direito de uma empresa associar sua marca ao nome de um espaço ou equipamento. Nesse caso, a empresa vencedora poderá fazer a associação nas condições previstas no edital e no contrato.

Segundo a Prefeitura, a medida busca atrair investimentos privados e gerar novas receitas para o município. A administração municipal afirma que o acordo não representa privatização, transferência da propriedade ou mudança da denominação oficial do teatro , que continuará sob responsabilidade da Prefeitura.

A secretária municipal de Gestão Estratégica, Lívia Mendes, afirmou que a proposta busca ampliar os investimentos na área cultural por meio de parcerias com a iniciativa privada.

O projeto foi desenvolvido pelas secretarias municipais de Cultura e Turismo e de Gestão Estratégica e está alinhado à Lei Municipal nº 14.409/2025, que prevê instrumentos de parceria para valorização e aproveitamento econômico de bens públicos.

Projetado pelo arquiteto Oscar Niemeyer e inaugurado em 2012, o Teatro Municipal é um dos principais equipamentos culturais e arquitetônicos de Uberlândia.

O espaço tem capacidade para 781 espectadores na área interna. Já a estrutura externa permite a abertura do palco para apresentações em formato de anfiteatro, com capacidade para receber cerca de 20 mil pessoas na praça.

O complexo ocupa uma área de 66,6 mil metros quadrados e tem aproximadamente 5 mil metros quadrados de área construída. A estrutura conta com camarins, salas de apoio, estacionamento e recursos de acessibilidade, como elevadores, rampas e espaços reservados para pessoas com deficiência.

articles.title: ‘Ramayana: Part 1’ box office collection Day 12: Ranbir Kapoor and Yash’s epic closes in on Rs 800 crore mark, earns Rs 32 crore on second Monday
articles.summary: ‘Ramayana’ is having a golden run at the box office.
articles.body: ‘Ramayana’ is having a golden run at the box office. Even in its second week, the mythological epic, led by Ranbir Kapoor as Lord Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita, and Yash as Ravana, is filling seats across the country. The Hindi version remains in the lead, while the dubbed releases have only boosted its pan-India numbers. While the film's daily earnings have slowed down, it's gross total keeps climbing, and several big milestones are now within reach.Ramayana Movie Review‘Ramayana day 12’ collection and language-wise breakupAccording to Sacnilk, ‘Ramayana’ earned Rs 32 crore net in India on day 12, spread over 22,365 shows. The Hindi version contributed Rs 23.75 crore from 17,742 screenings. Malayalam came next at Rs 2.85 crore across 1,061 shows, followed by Kannada with Rs 2 crore from 892 shows. Tamil collected Rs 1.90 crore from 1,158 shows, and Telugu rounded things off with Rs 1.50 crore from 1,512 shows.Compared to day 11, the film’s earnings fell by 57.3%, but its overall performance is still solid. articles.title: Lawsuit Accusing Selena Gomez and Wondermind Co-Founders of Fraud Is Dismissed
articles.summary: A lawyer for Gomez said the star "looks forward to putting the matter behind her"
articles.body:
A lawsuit accusing Selena Gomez, her mother Mandy Teefey, and The Newsette founder, Daniella Pierson, of defrauding investors behind the mental health startup Wondermind has been dropped after her attorneys filed a motion to dismiss the case.

"Selena is pleased by today's dismissal of the case following our motion to dismiss and looks forward to putting the matter behind her," her lawyer Mathew S. Rosengart said in a statement to Rolling Stone. According to documents, the plaintiffs "voluntarily" dismissed the lawsuit.

An attorney for Pierson, Scott Balber, told Billboard that they did not pay any settlement in the case. "Ms. Pierson did nothing wrong," said Balber. "Apparently, the plaintiff recognized that and dismissed the complaint against her. Unfortunately, Ms. Pierson's reputation has already been damaged by these false allegations. We are hopeful that the dismissal of the lawsuit will be the first step in restoring her good name."

In August, Gomez, Teefey, and Pierson were sued by investors claiming they pumped nearly $1.2 million into Wondermind, which launched in 2021, and were fed false promises about the company's infrastructure, leadership, and resources as the company collapsed. The trio, who founded the startup, were sued for securities fraud, common law fraud, and breach of contract.

In the lawsuit, investors alleged they were led to believe that a groundbreaking Wondermind app would be made, advertising deals would be struck, and celebrity cover stories were pending. Instead, the complaint claimed, "for three years, while the Company quietly collapsed around them, not one of its founders, officers, or directors said a word to the investors whose money was funding the collapse."

In the motion to dismiss, Gomez's legal team said she should have never been dragged into the case in the first place. Her lawyers added that while the star "agreed to support her mother Mandy Teefey" and invested in and holds a minority stake in Wondermind, Gomez "never agreed to and did not manage" the company.

In a previous statement to Rolling Stone , Rosengart said the claims against her were "completely meritless if not frivolous." He added, "The notion that Selena engaged in 'fraud' or any other wrongdoing is absurd—and in addition to filing our motion we are exploring other avenues of relief for Ms. Gomez including sanctions against plaintiffs for improperly including her."

articles.title: Queen of crime drama, Lynda La Plante, haunted by Rentaghost role
articles.summary: The author reflects on the unlikely encounters that helped shape her early crime dramas.
articles.body:
Screenwriter Lynda La Plante may be known as the "queen of crime drama", but it is a role in a cult children's TV series that audiences also remember her for.

La Plante appeared in five episodes in the classic series Rentaghost in 1980, playing nanny Tamara Novek, before finding fame as the creator of Prime Suspect.

Speaking ahead of an appearance at the Folkestone Book Festival, the 83-year-old said: "It has haunted me.

"I remember very clearly the director telling me, 'Oh for goodness' sake, it'll only be a little thing - nobody is going to notice.'"

La Plante said when she was giving lectures at Cambridge and Oxford, she was asked if she had starred in Rentaghost.

"It's unbelievable. It's followed me everywhere," she said.

Before turning to screenwriting, the Rada-trained actress built a successful acting career.

She appeared alongside Anthony Hopkins in repertory theatre, and took roles in television dramas including Coronation Street and The Sweeney.

La Plante said it was acting that helped shape her writing and create the gritty crime dramas that have cemented her reputation.

While writing her first television script, La Plante said a member of the props department introduced her to the criminal underworld, which influenced her later work.

The author said a meeting was arranged in a notorious London pub, where La Plante met her first murderer.

La Plante recalled the criminals spoke candidly about their lives.

"My acting training helped me relax and get people talking," she said.

La Plante said police officers were equally helpful and she urged aspiring writers to "go to the source".

"I've always advised writers don't make up things, you need to speak to real people [and learn about their experiences]."

Those encounters helped her formulate dramas including Widows and Prime Suspect, which ran for seven series, won multiple Baftas and sold to 196 territories worldwide.

From prisons to police stations, La Plante sought first-hand accounts to inform her writing.

Among those she met was notorious criminal Charles Bronson , with whom she exchanged letters while he was at Wakefield prison.

Alongside her television work, La Plante has written 50 bestselling-novels and sold more than five million books in the UK.

In 2024, she received the Diamond Dagger, crime writing's highest honour.

Her latest novel, Sudden Death, is her first standalone book in more than a decade.

Inspired by both the House of Romanov and the death of her beloved Borzoi dog, Hugo, it will be among the topics she is due to discuss at this month's Folkestone Book Festival.

articles.title: LCD Soundsystem to headline Platt Fields Park gigs in 2027
articles.summary: The Manchester park will host a series of 25,000-capacity concerts over two weekends next summer.
articles.body:
Large outdoor concerts are due to return to Manchester's Platt Fields Park next summer, with LCD Soundsystem named as the first headliner.

The American rock band will perform at the park in Fallowfield on 30 July 2027, with Young Fathers, Cowboy Hunters and DJs Erol Alkan and Luka Una also on the bill.

Organisers said the concert would be part of a series of shows, each with a capacity of 25,000, taking place over two weekends in late July and early August.

The events, called PlattForm, are being organised by The Warehouse Project, SJM Concerts and Live Nation, with more artists due to be announced in the coming weeks.

Platt Fields Park previously hosted the Parklife music festival from 2010 to 2012, before it moved to Heaton Park in 2013 to accommodate growing crowds.

Other music festivals have since taken place at the park, including Flashback Festival in 2022 and 2023.

Sam Kandel, founder of The Warehouse Project and an event director, said the park had its "own unique character", shaped by its location and surrounding communities.

Councillor Shazia Butt, Manchester City Council's executive member for culture, leisure and libraries, welcomed the announcement.

She said the council would work closely with organisers to ensure "maximum benefit for Platt Fields and for the local community", with further information expected in the coming months.

Tickets for the LCD Soundsystem concert go on general sale on Friday 20 November.

articles.title: ‘Cliff Booth’ First Reactions: Brad Pitt’s Sequel Is an ‘Absolute Triumph’ and a ‘Wildly Entertaining’ ‘Love Letter’ to Hollywood
articles.summary: David Fincher, Brad Pitt and Quentin Tarantino’s long-awaited “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” sequel movie, officially titled “The Further Mis-Adventures of...
articles.body:
David Fincher, Brad Pitt and Quentin Tarantino's long-awaited "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" sequel movie, officially titled "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth," has been unveiled to members of the film press, who are calling the Netflix-backed tentpole a "wildly entertaining" "hangout movie" that is already one of the year's best.

"David Fincher's The Further Mis-Adventures of #CliffBooth pops, throbs and crackles," wrote film critic Simon Thompson. "Like Once Upon a Time… this is a love letter to LA. An eclectic, ragtag cast make this a slick and sexy romp. A salty and slower-burning side piece to Tarantino's original with a fire final act."

Tomatometer critic Zach Pope called the film "a PURE cinematic trifecta of Tarantino's signature chaos, Fincher's meticulous attention to detail, and Brad Pitt's effortlessly charismatic Cliff Booth."

He continued: "All wrapped into a stylish love letter to 1970s Hollywood cinema that reminds us sometimes all you need is a laid-back, wildly entertaining misadventure with a character you just LOVE spending time with. That just might turn into insanity. It's cool, chaotic, charming, and never tries to be more than it needs to be. If you loved Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, this one's absolutely for you. Just as it was for me."

The Wrap's Senior Film Reporter Drew Taylor "absolutely loved" the film. "Tarantino and Fincher are like peanut butter and chocolate (the peanut butter is profane and the chocolate dipped in blood). Stop watching anything, go see it on the biggest screen around, have the time of your life. An absolute triumph. The best," he wrote .

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is an absolute banger," wrote Critics Choice member Ricky Válero. "An aesthetically rich film that beautifully captures the relationship between Los Angeles and the movies. Brad Pitt is as charismatic as ever. Truly one of the year's best films."

Variety's Clayton Davis described the film as a "wild, hilarious hangout movie." "Brad Pitt slides back into his beloved Oscar-winning role and gives his best performance since "Once Upon a Time in…Hollywood." Elizabeth Debicki brings an intoxicating sensuality, and Scott Caan and Peter Weller are such a treat that they could have had triple the screen time," he continued. "The cinematography is gorgeous. If the 2019 film was a love letter to L.A., this one is a full-on sonnet.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" features the return of Pitt as the eponymous stuntman. The movie is set in 1977, eight years after the events of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," and follows Cliff as a Hollywood studio fixer who gets in way over his head while working for a popular movie actor. The supporting cast includes Brad Pitt, Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Carla Gugino and Peter Weller, among others.

Pitt won the Oscar for best supporting actor for playing Cliff Booth in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," which Sony released in theaters in June 2019. The movie was acclaimed and earned a strong $410 million at the worldwide box office. "Hollywood" went on to earn 10 Oscar nominations, including best picture and best director.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" features a screenplay by Tarantino, who opted not to direct the movie because, per his retirement plan, he only plans on directing one more feature film before he leaves the director's chair for good. The first draft of the sequel script clocked in at a whopping 230 pages, Fincher revealed to Empire magazine last month. The director cut 60 pages.

articles.title: Bob Dylan's hooded Vatican visit with Pope Leo shows he's still knockin' on heaven's door
articles.summary: Bob Dylan met Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican, keeping his hood up as the first Augustinian friar to be elected pope called himself a son of St. Augustine.
articles.body: I was not surprised to see legendary singer and songwriter Bob Dylan (born Robert Zimmerman) visiting Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican a few weeks ago, dressed in what looked to be nomadic garb. He reportedly insisted on keeping his hood up, and the pope agreed. Perhaps Dylan was channeling his apocalyptic song "All Along the Watchtower," which describes the fall of Babylon prophesied in the eighth century (Isaiah 21) before taking place in 539 B.C. Or perhaps he was taking on the role of a hooded healer to the pope, who had just recovered from lung cancer surgery. It is no secret that Pope Leo, who hails from Chicago, is a longtime fan of Dylan’s, another Midwesterner who was born in Duluth, Minnesota. In July 2026, the pope wrote the preface for a Vatican book called "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift." In it, he quoted from Dylan’s unreleased 1963 Cold War protest song, "Go Away You Bomb": "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an’ man-handled." At the meeting with Dylan, the pope pointed to his Augustinian background (he is the first Augustinian friar to be elected pope) and introduced himself as a "son of St. Augustine." This was no doubt a direct reference to Dylan’s 1967 song, "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine." POPE LEO VISITS SITE OF MIRACLE CURES, MEETS PEOPLE WHOSE UNEXPLAINED HEALINGS STUNNED DOCTORS According to Dylan’s longtime Chabad rabbi, Manis Friedman, Dylan is a spiritual seeker. "The answer is blowin’ in the wind," Friedman told me for my new book, "The Angels Among Us," "but Dylan hasn’t found it yet. He’s knockin’ on heaven’s door, but can’t get in." Indeed, Dylan’s deep spiritual journeys and investigations reflect this "seeking" as he ranges from Orthodox Judaism to evangelical Christianity (he famously saw Jesus in a hotel room in 1978 and studied the New Testament intensely with his then-girlfriend, Mary Alice Artes, from 1978 to 1980). DR. MARC SIEGEL: 'THE ANGELS AMONG US' -- A DYING WOMAN, THE SHOFAR AND THE MIRACLE THAT FOLLOWED During this born-again Christian period, Dylan produced his celebrated album "Slow Train Coming," including the hit song "Gotta Serve Somebody," followed by "Every Grain of Sand" on his album "Shot of Love." But while Dylan was studying the New Testament, he was introduced to Rabbi Friedman as well as the famed Rebbe (Rabbi Menachem Schneerson), and Dylan then refocused his studies to include the Old Testament. As I write in my new book, he asked Rabbi Friedman, "What does infidel mean? He liked the word, kept asking about it. Infidel? What did I think of it?" CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND Dylan was once again questioning and reforming his spiritual identity, this time more toward Orthodox Judaism. The album "Infidels" followed in 1983, including the song "Jokerman," about a worker of blasphemous magic, more of an Antichrist than a godlike figure. One of Dylan’s best friends from childhood was Larry Kegan, who was paralyzed in a cliff-diving accident at age 16 but managed to survive as he said a prayer directly to God. He spent the rest of his life as a psychotherapist giving back to God and humanity, and he became Bob Dylan’s angel, often appearing with him at concerts in a wheelchair. As I describe in "The Angels Among Us," when Dylan, Larry and a third friend visited the Rebbe, with thousands in the room, everyone ignored the famous Dylan as the Rebbe had eyes only for Larry. The Rebbe raised a glass and wished Larry Kegan a long life. Dylan was humbled, saying he needed to work on his soul so he could become more worthy of recognition. POPE LEO WELCOMED BACK AS HE DELIVERS ANGELUS PRAYER DAYS AFTER LUNG CANCER SURGERY This meeting with the pope wasn’t Dylan’s first. In 1997, he nearly died of a severe infection known as pericardial histoplasmosis, especially difficult for a smoker to recover from. Coincidentally, Dylan recorded his near-death song, "Not Dark Yet," months before he got sick. A few months after he recovered, Dylan met with Pope John Paul II in Bologna, Italy, a meeting that Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger (the future Pope Benedict XVI) tried to block because, as he wrote later in his memoirs, he considered rock stars like Dylan to be the wrong kind of "prophet" for Christian youth. But Pope John Paul II overruled him, and Dylan performed several songs, including "Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION After the performance, the pope addressed the crowd and took on the very question that Dylan raised in "Blowin’ in the Wind" that Rabbi Friedman mentioned. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The pope had a definitive answer: "A representative of yours has spoken for you, saying that the answer is 'blowin' in the wind.' It is true! But not in the wind that blows things away in a whirlwind of nothingness. The wind that is the breath and voice of the Spirit, a voice that calls and says: 'Come!' You asked me: how many roads must a man walk down before you can call him a man? I answer you: one! There is only one road for man, and it is the road of Jesus Christ, who said, 'I am the way.'" articles.title: Jim Gaffigan, New York lawmakers push Gov Hochul to axe 'unnecessary tax' hitting comedy clubs
articles.summary: Comedian Jim Gaffigan joined New York lawmakers and club owners at a Manhattan rally, urging Gov. Kathy Hochul to sign a bill ending state sales tax on comedy clubs.
articles.body: New York’s comedy clubs are demanding an end to an "unnecessary" sales tax on comedy tickets that they say threatens to price out everyday fans, and comedian Jim Gaffigan helped lead the charge on Thursday. The New York State Legislature unanimously passed a bill in June that would exempt comedy performances from the state’s sales tax on admissions, a break already enjoyed by Broadway theaters, concert halls and even bowling alleys. The legislation now awaits action by Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, and advocates are calling on her to sign it before the end of the year, arguing the tax is putting additional financial pressure on the state’s comedy industry. BILL MAHER RIPS CALIFORNIA TAXES, SAYS STATE TAKES BIGGER CUT THAN A 'SKEEZY' DRUG DEALER "It really comes down to comedians need people to be able to afford to go to a show," Gaffigan exclusively told Fox News Digital during a rally at The Stand comedy club in Manhattan on Thursday. "And [not having] this unnecessary tax that Broadway shows don't have to deal with makes it more palatable for someone to pay," he added. "And particularly given the economic times, people might come out, but if they see the sales tax, even if it moves the bill up a little bit, that might dissuade them from coming back." Club owners and supporters of the legislation argue that the tax is a legal oversight, dating back to a time when New York City's comedy industry was less established and stand-up performances weren't treated the same as other performing arts. JOHN RICH WARNS NASHVILLE'S FAMED BROADWAY COULD GO DARK AS BUSINESSES FACE TAX ‘DEATH NAIL’ Paul Italia, co-owner of The Stand and the newly-opened The Stand West, pointed to the difference in how the same comedy performance can be taxed depending on the venue. He argued that if Gaffigan performed at his club and then delivered the same set at a venue classified as a theater later in the week, customers at The Stand would have to pay sales tax, while those at the theater would not. "There was a gray area, and a lot of us have not been collecting sales tax. And recently, the state decided to come — I don't want to say come after us — but in audits, this has come up many times," Italia told Fox News Digital. "We are being asked to pay for money that we never collected, because we never charged the sales tax, some of us, and that hurts a great deal," he added. "In fact, if it continues to go that way, I think it would cause a bit of a strain on some of our businesses, comedy clubs, that we may not be able to overcome." HOLLYWOOD STAR SOUNDS ALARM OVER DISAPPEARING JOBS AS PRODUCTIONS FLEE CALIFORNIA Movie theaters, the circus and even singles networking events can all claim tax-exempt status, while comedy clubs cannot, according to New York Assemblymember Keith Powers (D), who sponsored the Assembly version of the bill. Powers told Fox News Digital that vague rules have left small venues vulnerable to surprise tax audits and a "gigantic financial liability" that could force clubs to shut their doors. "I can't defend why comedy clubs would be left out of it if everyone else is receiving it, so why not now?" Powers said. Democratic New York state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez, a self-described democratic socialist who sponsored the Senate bill, called the measure "common sense" and joked about the irony of a democratic socialist pushing to eliminate a tax. She urged Hochul to "sign the bill, please." FORGET PAYING YOUR ‘FAIR SHARE’ OF TAXES. HERE ARE 5 WAYS POLITICIANS WANT EVEN MORE "As much as I'm a democratic socialist, and I was able to make that joke … I also think it's fair to support our small businesses, our artists and, that as a state representative of a district that has so many of them, this is part of my job and duty to my constituents," Gonzalez told Fox News Digital. Gaffigan added that New York City is an "artistic community" where comedy plays an important role and said he believes Hochul recognizes its significance. "New York City is very important for stand-up comedy, so I selfishly want that to be fed and supported," Gaffigan said. "I think that Governor Hochul understands that."
